content: This guideline provides a global, evidence-based recommendation on the use of multiple micronutrient powders for point-of-use fortification of foods consumed by pregnant women. Pregnant women are particularly vulnerable to vitamin and mineral deficiencies due to increased metabolic demands required to support fetal growth and development. Globally, approximately 42% of pregnant women aged 15–49 years are anemic, with iron deficiency anemia accounting for about 60% of these cases in non-malarial areas and 50% in malaria-endemic regions. Deficiencies in vitamins and minerals during pregnancy are associated with adverse health outcomes for both the mother and the neonate. The purpose of this guideline is to assist Member States in making evidence-informed decisions regarding appropriate nutrition interventions to improve the nutritional status of pregnant women. It also aims to support efforts to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals, the global targets outlined in the Comprehensive Implementation Plan on Maternal, Infant, and Young Child Nutrition, and the Global Strategy for Women’s, Children’s, and Adolescents’ Health (2016–2030). The guideline is intended for a broad audience, including governments, non-governmental organizations, healthcare workers, scientists, and donors involved in designing and implementing micronutrient programs and antenatal care services, as well as integrating these into national and subnational public health strategies. The World Health Organization (WHO) developed this evidence-informed recommendation using the procedures outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. The process included identifying priority questions and outcomes, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for dissemination, implementation, and evaluation. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) methodology was used to prepare evidence profiles based on systematic reviews. The guideline development group consisted of content experts, methodologists, and representatives of stakeholders and beneficiaries. The systematic review included two trials. One trial, involving 478 pregnant women, compared micronutrient powders for point-of-use fortification of foods with iron and folic acid supplements. The other trial, involving 470 pregnant women, compared micronutrient powders with the same multiple micronutrients in supplement form. Both trials were conducted in rural settings, one in Bangladesh and the other in Mexico, and neither was in a malaria-endemic area. The overall quality of evidence was very low, and no evidence was available for most critical and important outcomes. The recommendation states that the routine use of multiple micronutrient powders during pregnancy is not recommended as an alternative to standard iron and folic acid supplementation for improving maternal and infant health outcomes. This strong recommendation is based on very low-quality evidence and reflects the limited data available to directly assess the potential benefits or harms of using point-of-use fortification with multiple micronutrient powders in pregnant women. Evidence to date shows no added value of multiple micronutrient powders over iron and folic acid supplementation in pregnant women. An efficient system for routine data collection, including therapeutic adherence and program performance measures, is critical to ensure the effectiveness and sustainability of supplementation programs, particularly for iron and folic acid supplementation. Monitoring is essential to identify barriers that may sustain unequal access to antenatal care, including iron and folic acid supplementation. Sustained implementation and scale-up efforts benefit significantly from appropriate monitoring mechanisms. The WHO Secretariat will continue to monitor research developments in the area of micronutrient supplementation for pregnant women. If the guideline requires an update or if concerns arise regarding its validity, the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development will coordinate the update following the formal procedures outlined in the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development. As the guideline approaches its 10-year review period, the Department of Nutrition for Health and Development at WHO headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, along with its internal partners, will conduct a search for new evidence. WHO welcomes suggestions for additional questions to evaluate in the guideline when it is due for review.
